rows.en: One example of the understanding of the statutes in those days will show us clearly that they were not then strict about the meaning of the words as written, so that at times they departed from the sense of the statute and applied it in a particular way, against its plain meaning in the Torah; and this is a sign of a reasoned understanding. This example will appear to us in what is told of David when he came to Ahimelech the priest at Nob, the city of the priests. David asked him for bread for his men, and the priest did not withhold from him the holy bread that he had at hand, since he had no other bread besides it. He gave him the showbread that had been removed from before the Lord, but on condition that they had kept themselves from women (1 Samuel 21). Now if we ask what the sense of the Torah's statute is in this matter, we must say that from the statute in the Torah there is no proof in any way that this bread may be eaten by non-priests, even if they are clean. For it says explicitly: "And it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat it in a holy place" [Leviticus 24:9]. How then shall we reconcile this with the story before us? We are forced to say that in those days they decided the matter thus: once the showbread had already been removed from before the Lord, its holiness was lessened, so that it was permitted to clean non-priests. And this is surely a departure from the plain sense of the statute in the Torah (see Menaḥot 95).

The new thing that Samuel created in the land, founding the Naioth in Ramah to educate the youths of Israel in the Torah of the Lord, was the foundation on which the house of Israel would establish its happiness and its survival in the times to come.⚠1 These Naioth were a blessed source from which the springs of faith and of the knowledge of the Lord would spread in every generation, for from them came the sons of the prophets. They were at all times among the men faithful to the covenant of the Lord, without partiality. They served faithfully on the holy soil, and they were called to proclaim the word of the Lord. Both the priests and the kings turned aside time after time from the way of the Torah, but the prophets did not turn aside. This is the course of the spirit that moves through all the events of the days of the kings up to the exile of the land. Had the prophets not stood up for their people, the Torah would then have perished. And if through all the days of the First Temple we find a slackness in its observance, so that in the days of King Josiah's reign it was actually forgotten, to whom shall this iniquity be reckoned? Only to the priests, who were called to keep the charge of the Torah and profaned their office. They were appointed to teach the people its statutes, but they did the work of the Lord falsely and deceitfully. From the very beginning the Torah of God was given into their hands. The book of the Torah was placed in the Tabernacle of the Testimony beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord (Deuteronomy 31:26); and when Joshua set a statute and an ordinance in Shechem and wrote these words in the book of the Torah of the Lord,{v1_02_20:1} he placed them likewise in the sanctuary (Joshua 24). For it was an ancient custom among most nations in ancient times to deposit their holy writings in the temples of their gods.{v1_02_20:2} So it was also in the Temple that Solomon built, which called one part of the house "the devir of the house," because the word [davar] of the Lord was placed in it.{v1_02_20:3} Of the book of the Torah there was a copy in the hand of the king and also in the hand of the priests. The copy in the priests' hand was kept in the Temple court and was called "the book of the Court," and from it they would correct all the copies (Mo'ed Katan 18b; Yerushalmi Shekalim 4:5 and Sanhedrin 2:4). Now it is self-evident that the priests in charge of the House were also charged with keeping the book (Deuteronomy 31); the king's copy too was made from the one before the Levitical priests (ibid. 17:18), and they were called to teach the statutes of the Lord (ibid. 16:9)⚠2; and this office continued until a very late time. The prophet Jeremiah describes the office of the priests as the teaching of the Torah, and that of the prophets as having the word of the Lord in their mouth (Jeremiah 18:18). And so it is described also in the book of Malachi (2:7). But how did they keep their charge? On this the prophets tell us that they transgressed their covenant and did violence to the Torah, caused many to stumble in the Torah, and taught for hire. And they said: "those who handle the Torah did not know" the Lord [Jeremiah 2:8]; and those who handle the Torah are none other than the priests. And the prophet Jeremiah suspected them of falsifying the Torah, when he said: "How do you say, We are wise, and the Torah of the Lord is with us? Behold, the false pen of the scribes has made it into a lie" (Jeremiah 5:8)⚠3. Yet for the most part they did not corrupt their way out of wickedness of heart, but out of a weakness of moral strength to stand against kings; and at every time and in every place where the kings corrupted their way, the priests too could not hold back, and went with the kings after vanity and became vain. And when the king set his heart to his God, the hand of the priests too was with him. In the time of King Jehoshaphat, who walked in the commandments of his God, he appointed some of the priests and the Levites to teach the people knowledge and Torah (2 Chronicles 17); and Hezekiah strengthened the hand of the priests so that they too would hold fast to the Torah of the Lord (ibid. 31:4). But this was a crooked way, and it led only to want; for when the priests did evil in turning aside, they did not do good in returning, since they did not return from the heart. And they still went in this way in the days of the exile. For instead of keeping the Torah of the Lord in their mouths and turning many from iniquity, as they were charged, they turned from the way and caused many to stumble in the Torah, and so corrupted the covenant of Levi (Malachi 2:6–5)⚠4. Even the high priest Joshua, who was set up at the beginning of the Second Temple, was not free of every blemish, as appears from the prophet's visions directed at him (Zechariah 3); and he was not held to be clean of guilt as befits a high priest (Sanhedrin 93a, and Song of Songs Rabbah on the verse "I rose"). All the more so the priests who lived in the days of the exile in the land of Judah, who did not separate themselves from the nations of the land but mixed with them and were profaned (Ezra 9:11). But the remnant whom the Lord calls were the prophets. Even in the land of the Ten Tribes the prophets stood guard over the religion, from the time the kingdom was divided in the days of Jeroboam until the exile of the land in the days of Hoshea son of Elah. And they drew some of the people after them, so that even among the servants of Ahab's wicked kingdom there were those who feared the Lord (1 Kings 18). And many thousands of the people had their heart whole with the Lord (ibid. 19), and many in Israel were found who went to the prophet on the Sabbath and on the new moon to inquire of the Lord (2 Kings 4:23); and in the days of Elisha the elders sat before him, and their hand was steady with him, and they did their deeds according to the Torah. So in every generation the prophets stood at their post and kept the religion and the Torah. And in truth we owe thanks for the survival of the Torah to them alone. And for that reason this remained firm in the belief of the people: that the chain of transmission of the Torah went from Moses to Joshua, from Joshua to the elders, from the elders to the prophets, and the prophets handed it to the Men of the Great Assembly (Avot 1:1), and there is no mention of the priests; although it cannot be denied in any way that the priests were the first recipients, as it is said: "And Moses wrote this Torah and gave it to the priests the Levites" [Deuteronomy 31:9]. This can only be because they knew clearly that the priests broke the statute and changed the teachings and did not hold the chain of tradition; only the prophets held it. Now we have seen from all this how great was the effect of the prophet Samuel on all the generations to come. For in founding the Naioth to educate the sons of his people in the ways of the Torah, he was the cause of the strengthening of the religion in all the times to come; these Naioth were an open source from which prophecy went forth, and the men who were its bearers were also the bearers of the Torah in every generation. For this reason the sages after him recognized the greatness of his worth and rank, so that they set him on the level of Moses (Jeremiah 15:1); and in later generations too they said that Samuel was equal to Moses and Aaron (Numbers Rabbah ch. 18 and Exodus Rabbah ch. 15). And for that reason we find that from his time on the traces of the Torah multiply in the books meant to tell the events of his time and after it.

rows.en: From the time of David to the time of the destruction of the Temple.

The pleasant plantings that Samuel planted in the vineyard of the Lord of hosts grew quickly and prospered, and also bore fruit. The blossoms of holy poetry appeared in the land, and the song of the Lord opened upon it like a lily. The psalms and hymns handed down to us in the name of David king of Israel, and the sublime poems that the poets of his time sang, were glorious in holy splendor. The spirit of the Torah of Moses spoke in them, and they were lifted up by the fear of the Lord. Therefore it is very likely that that time was more wonderful in this respect too than the times that had passed, in that they set their heart to meditate on the Torah of God. And how shall we turn to this? When we see how very exalted this king was in holding fast to the Torah and making it the measuring line in all his deeds. In his last words, when he charged Solomon his son, his command to him was: "keep the charge of the Lord your God, to walk in His ways, to keep His statutes and His commandments, His judgments and His testimonies, as it is written in the Torah of Moses" (1 Kings 2:3). And if he sometimes departed from the statute of the Torah, this was only because of a momentary weakness of his soul. And although in all the stories we have of his life and deeds there are only very few traces of the Torah's statutes, this is not a sign that inquiry into them was lacking, but because the narrator found no place or reason to mention them. Yet for all that, traces of great value for our purpose are scattered across the stories of his life and of the lives of the kings after him. Thus it is told that David sentenced the Amalekite stranger to death because he confessed of himself that he had killed Saul. Likewise he condemned Rechab and Baanah to death on their own confession. Now if we could know that David did so and decided their case according to the law of the Torah in capital cases, we could draw from this a conclusion about the nature of the law of conviction at that time, and say that the confession of the party was sufficient testimony to decide a death sentence on it. But who knows this? Perhaps David acted so as an emergency measure and not according to law.{v1_03_02:1} But we should pay attention to one expression that the narrator uses and puts in David's mouth, namely what he said to the Amalekite stranger: "Your blood be upon your head, for your mouth has testified against you, saying, I have slain the Lord's anointed" (2 Samuel 1:15)⚠1. Now it is all one to us whether David really said it or not; in any case this expression that the writer uses is very old, and its origin is from the days of the kings (see below, ch. 4). And from its form it appears that "your mouth has testified against you" was a common expression for a person's testimony against himself, and its sense is that the confession of a party counts as witnesses. Such expressions never arise except through use as a common thing.⚠2 Therefore there was surely an established law that the confession of the sinner's own mouth is a full testimony [aniyah], and aniyah is nothing but testimony. For the word anah is a fixed and technical term in the law of the Torah for the notion of testimony, as in "You shall not bear [ta'aneh] false witness against your neighbor" [Exodus 20:13], and likewise "to testify against him [la'anot bo] of wrongdoing" [Deuteronomy 19:16].{v1_03_02:2} Now the expression "your mouth has testified against you", whose meaning is that his mouth is the witness against himself, necessarily shows that at the time this expression was used there was a fixed law that a man's mouth and his confession are as witnesses in capital cases. And this principle agrees with the foundations of the law of all lawgivers, ancient and recent, down to our time, among all of whom the most trustworthy testimony was a person's testimony about himself, namely the confession of his mouth. And if we consider the words of the Torah that speak of witnesses in capital cases, we find that they can be explained in this direction in a fitting way; and no doubt the words of the Torah's law were understood so, in agreement with the expression mentioned, in the time of our earliest ancestors, and they thought that when the law of the Torah says "Whoever kills a person, the murderer shall be put to death at the mouth of witnesses; but one witness shall not testify against a person that he die" (Numbers 35), and likewise "At the mouth of two witnesses ... shall he that is to die be put to death; he shall not be put to death at the mouth of one witness" (Deuteronomy 17), it does not mean by this to exclude one who confesses of himself. For no special statute is needed for one who confesses of himself, since about one who confesses that he killed a person there is no doubt of the truth of the matter. But since for the most part a murderer does not confess of himself, and one must rely on the testimony of witnesses, Scripture speaks of the usual case, to judge by witnesses; and not to exclude one who confesses of himself, but to exclude a single witness. Therefore wherever it states that capital cases are to be decided by witnesses, its opposite is also stated explicitly, namely that they are not to be decided by one witness. Thus the meaning of the statute will be: at the mouth of two witnesses shall he that is to die be put to death, but not at the mouth of one witness. This is what it means to exclude, and not one who confesses of himself; for one who confesses, it is self-evident that we believe him, and all the more so. And this old interpretation has been preserved for us in an old aggadah (Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 6:1) that tells of Achan the Zarhite: Achan said to Joshua, "Do you catch me by a lot? Did not Moses our teacher teach us, 'at the mouth of two witnesses shall a matter be established'? You have already begun to err in judgment!" Joshua was afraid that they would bring an evil name upon the lots by which the land was to be divided; so Joshua began to appease Achan and to adjure him by the God of Israel, saying: "My son, give glory to the Lord God of Israel!" And Achan answered and said: "Indeed I have sinned!" (see Bavli Sanhedrin 43b and Numbers Rabbah ch. 23). It follows from the phrasing of these words that Achan's confession was considered as testimony and as proof of the matter in capital cases. On the other hand, we have not found even one incident from the time when they judged capital cases in which they refused to decide the case on the basis of a person's own confession. It is true that it is told of Simeon ben Shetaḥ (Sanhedrin 37b) that he ran after a man who was pursuing his fellow into a ruin, and saw a sword in the pursuer's hand dripping blood and the slain man writhing; Simeon said to him: "Wicked one, who killed this man, I or you? But what can I do, for the Torah said, 'at the mouth of two witnesses shall he that is to die be put to death.'" But there is no proof that if the murderer had confessed he would not have been sentenced to death; for what he said, "what can I do, for the Torah said, at the mouth of two witnesses shall he that is to die be put to death", means only this: since you do not confess, and there are no witnesses to the matter, I cannot sentence you to the death you deserve. However, halakhot have been handed down to us that teach that one is not put to death on a person's testimony about himself; and the clearest of them is what they said: "all those liable to death [are executed only] by a court, witnesses and warning" (Sanhedrin 80b; Tosefta ibid. ch. 10), the sense of their words being that it was said so precisely and to exclude self-confession. But for all that it appears clearly that as long as capital cases were judged, this opinion never became a matter of practice. Such opinions are only in the nature of theoretical opinions (theoriae), and did not come into practice; and this is because the later sages were opposed to the death penalty in general, as is said of R. Akiva and R. Tarfon (end of Makkot ch. 1). Only from the root of this wish to lighten the death penalties came various strange expositions founded on weak inferences; as when they say that if one of the things the Torah laid upon the witnesses cannot be fulfilled, as when the witnesses' hand is cut off, so that we cannot fulfil "the hand of the witnesses shall be first upon him" [Deuteronomy 17:7], then the death sentence of the accused is annulled (Sanhedrin 45a). And how strange are all the inferences they drew concerning the stubborn and rebellious son (ibid., Mishnah ch. 5)⚠3. Now surely from this root came also the rule that a man is not sentenced to death on his own confession, and all the details of the laws of the warning and of the acceptance of death.⚠4 But we have no means of bringing proof that a murderer was ever exempted from death although he confessed of himself, either because he had not been warned or because he had not accepted death upon himself. And in what follows we will succeed in bringing proof to the contrary.

rows.en: Also from the history of Solomon's reign a bright light shines for us on the subject of the Torah and religion. Solomon, on coming to the throne, kept the command of David his father with all care. When he blessed all the congregation of Israel at the dedication of the house he had built, this was the request he asked of his people: that their heart be whole with the Lord, to walk in His ways and to keep His statutes all the days, as on the day they stood before Him (1 Kings 8:61). So too the proverbs that he left behind as a blessing, which are with us in Scripture, bear upon them the spirit of the Torah of Moses. And although in the historical narratives of his time, too, the traces of the Torah are very few, it cannot be denied that this little is of great value by its character, and especially in that one sees in it that the line and measure in practice was the inquiry into the reason of the statutes. This character, engraved on those few traces, was without doubt the root of an old aggadah telling that King Solomon inquired into the reasons of the commandments and stumbled (Sanhedrin 21b). And so it truly was, as we shall see. Of the building of the house that Solomon built it is told: "And the house, when it was being built, was built of stone made ready at the quarry; and neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron was heard in the house while it was being built" (1 Kings 6:7). From the place of their quarrying they removed great stones to lay the foundation of the house, hewn stones, and they carved and prepared the stones for building the house (ibid. 5:31–32). We see from all this that he wanted to build the house of hewn stones; but they did the cutting and the dressing at the quarry, so that the sound of iron was not heard in the house, for everything had been prepared beforehand. There is no doubt that the narrator alludes here to the statute written in the Torah: "And if you make Me an altar of stones, you shall not build it of hewn stones" (Exodus 20:22), and "you shall not lift up any iron upon them" (Deuteronomy 27:5). But from the sense of this statute it appears that it warns against lifting iron only upon the stones of the altar; but for the house, even for the inner sanctuary of the house, which is the Holy of Holies, they were not warned about this (Mekhilta Yitro ch. 11). Yet from the matter told here it appears that it speaks of the house as a whole, that no hammer or axe was heard in it. It is further made clear to us from what it said, "was not heard in the house while it was being built," that it meant that it was not heard inside the house, but they dressed the stones outside and brought them in. So on the one side they widened the prohibition to the whole house, and on the other side they permitted making the stones hewn, only on condition that they be dressed outside (see Sotah 48b). This widening on the one side and the permission on the other will become known to us in their reason if we grasp the cause why iron may not be lifted upon the stones of the altar. And this cause is stated explicitly in the Torah, namely: because lifting iron causes the profanation of the altar. It is not as among the other peoples in ancient times, who held unhewn stones in honor, so that the ancient Greeks worshipped such stones (Pausanias 7.22.3); and the reason why unhewn stones were honored and esteemed among them was that they still stood in their natural state, as they came from the hand of the Maker (Knobel, Ex. 20:25). Not so the reason of the Torah; it is without doubt because iron is destined to be the instrument of destruction in war, while the altar is destined to be the place from which life and peace come (Tosefta Bava Kamma ch. 10; Bavli and Yerushalmi Kiddushin ch. 1). And not by chance does Scripture use the words "for if you lift up your sword upon it, you have profaned it" [Exodus 20:22], to hint that the purpose of the altar is the opposite of the purpose of iron, which is the sword.{v1_03_04:1} Therefore it is no wonder that this statute was widened to the whole Temple, for the very same reason for which lifting the sword upon the altar was forbidden, since the altar is part of the whole Temple and the purpose of both is one. But on the other side they saw the fulfillment of this reason only when the iron was brought into the interior of the Temple, and did not object to dressing the stones outside. Also at the dedication of the house that Solomon made we find that he departed greatly from the statute of the Torah, in a way whose ground we cannot know unless we decide that he permitted himself to depart because he had reached the depth of the Torah's intent and grasped its reason and purpose. For Solomon made the dedication of the altar seven days, joined to the Festival, which fell at that time for seven days, so that in that year they kept a festival that lasted fourteen days and ended on the twenty-second of the seventh month, for on the twenty-third he sent the people away (1 Kings 8:65; 2 Chronicles 7:9–10). From this it appears that the festival of consecration began on the ninth of the month, and the seventh day was already the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles, and after it came seven days with the festival of the Eighth Day, which is the Atzeret. It follows that they began to celebrate the festival on the ninth of the month, which is the beginning of the Day of Atonement, as the plain wording of the Torah indicates: "on the ninth day of the month at evening ... you shall keep your sabbath" [Leviticus 23:32]. And in that year they did not keep the Day of Atonement according to its rule (Mo'ed Katan 9a). Surely this was because for a purpose as great as the dedication of the altar and the Temple they did not hesitate to depart from the statute; especially since the dedication of the altar also has the function of atonement, to make atonement for it, so that it be most holy (Exodus 29:37), like the Day of Atonement, which is also appointed to atone, and especially for the holy sanctuary and the altar. For this reason he deliberately made the ninth the first day of the festival of consecration, and was obliged also to count the first day of the Feast of Tabernacles as the festival of the dedication of the altar.{v1_03_05:1} And who knows whether from that time on, in memory of that event which took place on the Day of Atonement, they did not also make the whole Day of Atonement a day of festival and joy, as it is told: there were no festive days for Israel like the fifteenth of Av and the Day of Atonement, on which the daughters of Israel would go out and dance in the vineyards; and they applied to it the verse "Go forth, O daughters of Zion, and behold King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding and on the day of the gladness of his heart" [Song of Songs 3:11]: "on the day of his wedding", this is the giving of the Torah; "and on the day of the gladness of his heart", this is the building of the Temple (Ta'anit 26b). Surely this refers only to the building of the Temple that Solomon built, when the Day of Atonement was a festival and a holiday; and for this reason they made the whole Day of Atonement a joy and a holiday, in memory of that Day of Atonement.

footnotes.en: The Masoretic reading in Samuel is: once "al ha-dam" [upon the blood] and once "el ha-dam" [to the blood], and both are one in intent. But according to the Septuagint translation, it is rendered in the Torah as if it were written "al he-harim" [upon the mountains], and in Samuel they translated as if it were written "et ha-dam" [the blood]. But we do not know the origin of this reading. For in saying "and they slaughtered on the ground" [1 Samuel 14:32], he indicates that they did not receive the blood in order to eat it, but that it was spilled on the ground. Therefore, if we emend to "et ha-dam," the word "on the ground" has no explanation; for he wanted to tell us on purpose that they slaughtered on the ground, and in this matter, that is, in slaughtering on the ground joined to eating the slaughtered animal in that place, lies the sin.⚠1 Whereas if they had eaten the blood, the slaughtering on the ground would neither add nor take away. Therefore the correct reading in Samuel is as we have it. And now it is self-evident that in the Torah too the true reading is that of the Masoretic text. For the words "Behold, the people are sinning by eating upon the blood" must refer to some statute, and it is no other statute than the one in the Torah; whereas if the reading were "upon the mountains," we would not know what the sin is in eating upon the blood.

1.note: Print unclear (looks like מתח ההטא); read מונח החטא, 'there lies the sin'.

footnotes.en: According to one of the sages of the Talmud, the Torah was given scroll by scroll (Gittin 60a); and from then on, when all the scrolls were put together,⚠1 they were called in Deuteronomy "the book of the Torah" (Deuteronomy 31). Those who say that "the book of the Torah" refers to Deuteronomy, or to particular parts that were written, and not to the whole Torah, must bring proof. It is not our purpose to argue about this. And see Bavli Makkot (11a), where R. Judah and R. Nehemiah disagree on what Joshua wrote in the book of the Torah of God: one says the eight verses, and the other says the cities of refuge. Now the one who says the eight verses clearly expounds against the plain sense of the words, for how would he explain "these words"? And according to the one who disputes him, the section of the cities of refuge was written by Joshua at the end of the days of conquest and settlement. The Talmud's resolution there is also against the sense of the verse. In any case, the argument of R. Meir in Sifre Deuteronomy, section 357 (or according to the Gemara, Bava Batra 15b and Zevaḥim 30a,⚠2 R. Simeon), that it is possible that Moses gave the Torah lacking one letter, is no argument; for according to other sages we see that it is indeed possible. This needs further study.

footnotes.en: See the introductions to Holy Scripture by Christian scholars, who brought proofs for this. Likewise the traveler Strabo relates (book 14, p. 734) that several nations he reached in his travels had the custom of depositing their holy writings in their temples. Likewise Eusebius relates (book 1, ch. 9) that a priest of Tyre wrote a chronicle of his people and his land, and drew his narratives from writings that were kept in their holy temple. See further what the scholar K. O. Müller⚠1 wrote on the writings of Sparta in his book (*Die Dorier*, vol. 2, p. 90), and likewise the historian of the Romans, Niebuhr (vol. 1, p. 526).

1.note: Initials printed ע. א.; taken as Karl Otfried Müller, author of Die Dorier.

footnotes.en: An example of the name "devir" in this sense is found elsewhere: "and the name of Debir before was Kiriath-sepher" (Joshua 15:15), which was no doubt so called because their holy writings were deposited there. See the *Book of Roots* by Dr. Julius Fürst, s.v. devir. And the Aramaic Targum renders Kiriath-sepher as "arkhei" [archives], whose meaning is a place where writings are kept; and in the Gemara (Avodah Zarah 24b) [it is said] that in Persian devir is a name for a book. Gesenius cites this, and a Christian commentator, one Keniaum,⚠1 copied it in his commentary on the book of Judges (1:17),⚠2 and said there that it is impossible to explain an old Hebrew word from the Persian language; and in this I agree with him. But I do not agree that he understood the intent of the Talmud, and without doubt he never saw it. For these are the words of the Talmud: "From where do the Persians call a book devir? From here: 'and the name of Debir before was Kiriath-sepher.'" Here we see that it did not occur to it to derive the Hebrew from the Persian, but on the contrary, that the Persians called a book devir after the Hebrew. And Kiriath-sepher is also called Kiriath-sannah (Joshua 15:49), which is also from the sense of learning, and its parallel is shinnen in the intensive conjugation (Fürst, s.v. shanan).

1.note: Name printed unclearly (OCR מיני אום); the commentator is not identified.

2.note: Debir is in Judges 1:11; kept as printed.

footnotes.en: Maimonides, in Hilkhot Melakhim 3:10, wrote that the king has authority to kill without clear proof and without witnesses. But this has no basis in the Torah, and it was founded only on incidents that took place; that is, since we saw that the kings actually did so, from this they judged that it is permitted to do so. But for the inquiry into antiquity such a judgment, from the later to the earlier, is no proof that the thing is right. And we must still ask: if the general statute was not so, why did they depart from it? And if we say that they were permitted, where is the permission written?

According to the scholar Shadal [S. D. Luzzatto], in his commentary on Isaiah 1:17, the sense of the verse "You shall not bear [ta'aneh]" etc. is: "You shall not answer [ta'aneh] your neighbor as a false witness"; and according to this interpretation there is no need to say that the root anah is a fixed term for the notion of testimony. But in the verse "to testify against him [la'anot bo] of wrongdoing [sarah]" one cannot add the word "as a witness" unless we explain that the word sarah describes the character of the witness's words, that is, that his words are sarah, and its sense is like "falsehood," as Luzzatto himself explained (ibid., verse 8).⚠1 But if we explain that the sense of sarah is the character of the deed that the sinner did, against whom he testified, and the intent of the verse is "to testify against him that he did wrong," then adding the word "as a witness" has no basis at all, and then the root anah necessarily means "testified." Indeed, if we consider the sequence of the verses in the Torah, we find that Luzzatto's interpretation is refuted. For these are the words of Scripture: "If a malicious witness rises up against a man to testify against him of wrongdoing, then both the men between whom the controversy is shall stand before the Lord ... and the judges shall inquire diligently, and behold, the witness is a false witness, he has testified falsely against his brother" (Deuteronomy 19:17–18). From this it appears that it means to say: if a witness testifies against a man that he committed a sin, and through the judges' inquiry it becomes known that what he testified is false. Hence sarah is necessarily a description of the sin and not of the character of the testimony, for the character of the testimony becomes known only through the judges' inquiry. Accordingly it is proved that the root anah in itself is a term for the notion of testimony. So also "and my righteousness will testify for me" [Genesis 30:33], and "our sins testify against us" [Isaiah 59:12].

1.note: The word סרה is in Isaiah 1:5; the figure may be ה rather than ח. Kept as read.
